source.title: Weight-sparse transformers have interpretable circuits
source.authors: Leo Gao; Achyuta Rajaram; Jacob Coxon; Soham V. Govande; Bowen Baker; Daniel P. Mossing

record.file_problem: The text contains some extraction artifacts and flattened figures, but the paper is legible and appears to include the full text.
record.tranche_reason: The paper tests whether pruned circuits can account for task behavior using a different method from the attribution-graph claim; the circuits are in weight-sparse models and contain several kinds of nodes.
record.gate_note: The paper does not audit neuron poles or score explanations on held-out activating examples. Its results on compact circuit size and qualitative feature interpretation do not measure the shares named in V1–V4 or the scoring in V6–V7. The bridge experiments perturb dense-model activations but do not report rates of a behavior or test attribution graphs. The pruned-circuit ablations do bear on the sufficiency of circuit units for task behavior in V5.
record.test_reason: The study does not test any version. Its models are small weight-sparse transformers trained de novo, with sparsity imposed on purpose to make circuits interpretable. It does not audit the shares of ordinary neurons (V1, V2, V4), study InceptionV1 (V3), build attribution graphs from a large model's own neurons (V5), or score explanations on held-out text (V6, V7). The pruned-circuit sufficiency and necessity tests (r4, r5) are on purpose-built sparse models, not on the kind of system V5 names. The dense-model bridge work uses trained bridges and reports steering effects only. The record's T2 and V5 'tests' should be dropped.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is essentially correct. The authors conclude that weight-sparse training yields compact, partly human-understandable circuits validated by mean ablation. Sparsity trades capability for interpretability, and scaling total parameters improves the frontier. Scaling beyond tens of millions of nonzero parameters remains hard, and bridges to dense models are preliminary.
record.recipe_differences: Uses weight-sparse training and task-specific node pruning with mean ablation, rather than auditing neuron poles or scoring explanations on new text.
record.method_sensitivity: Interpretability results vary with weight sparsity, model size, activation sparsity, and task complexity; the paper reports a capability–interpretability tradeoff as sparsity changes and improvement of the frontier with model scaling.

fits_no_version.finding: At matched pretraining loss, minimal pruned task circuits in weight-sparse models are about 16-fold smaller than in dense models.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Weight-sparse training yields far more compact task circuits than dense training at equal loss.

fits_no_version.finding: In weight-sparse models, retaining only the pruned circuit (other nodes mean-ablated) preserves task loss, and ablating the circuit severely harms it.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Circuits built from the native nodes of purpose-trained sparse models are sufficient and necessary for simple tasks under mean ablation.

fits_no_version.finding: Some but not all nodes are monosemantic on the pretraining distribution. Concepts are still smeared across nodes, though less than in dense models; random nodes are called 'somewhat interpretable'.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Weight sparsity reduces but does not eliminate polysemantic nodes.

record.problems: The qualitative node investigations cover three tasks across two models and include a cherry-picked monosemantic example. The authors state that mean ablation is not a perfect faithfulness measure and that full causal-scrubbing standards are not met. The models and tasks are limited in scale and scope.
record.rows_left_out: Dense-model bridge perturbations are not included because they report steering effects rather than the neuron-pole shares or held-out explanation scores in the claim versions. Other scaling and architecture plots report capability or circuit-size metrics that do not directly measure the listed versions.

untested.parts: All: no Qwen3-32B pole audit or shares.
All: no cross-model or scale shares of interpretable neurons.
All: no InceptionV1 or recursive-generalization analysis.
All. Weight sparsity is imposed by training, and no share of interpretable neurons is measured against architecture or tools.
All: no attribution graphs on a large ordinary model's own neurons, and no comparison against replacement-model reconstruction error.
All: no test of whether explanations predict firing beyond their activating examples.

missing.what: Qualitative statement that randomly selected nodes in sparse models seem somewhat interpretable (no proportion given)
missing.versions: none (related to V4 only loosely; sparsity is induced on purpose)

record.verdict_notes: This is an OpenAI paper on weight-sparse transformers. It assumes dense neurons are hard to interpret but does not measure that. It is relevant background for V4's architecture argument but is not a test, because interpretability is engineered and no neuron share is reported. The bridge experiments involve a trained mapping, the opposite of V5's no-replacement condition, and report only steering curves.

versions.untested_parts: Qwen3-32B pole-level audit and the stated percentages.
Shares across dense and mixture-of-experts models or up to trillions of parameters.
InceptionV1 cat-and-car example and recursive generalization.
Interpretable-neuron shares in Inception-sized vision models and the stated estimates.
Attribution graphs for a large model's own neurons, and the specific claim about avoiding a trained replacement model and its reconstruction error.
Whether explanations fit activating examples but fail to predict firing on new text.
Automated activation-simulation scores on new text.

rows.subject: weight-sparse model circuits
rows.operation_detail: Compared the size of minimal pruned circuits in sparse and dense models at matched pretraining loss.

conditions.value: hand-curated task suite; average across tasks

rows.measure: Pruned circuit size, measured by number of edges
rows.baseline: Dense model with the same pretraining loss
rows.value: Sparse model circuits are roughly 16-fold smaller at any given loss.
rows.note: This measures task-specific circuit compactness, not a share of interpretable neuron poles.
rows.check: Circuit-size comparison against a dense model. This is a selection or comparison of the study's own method, not a share of interpretable neurons.

rows.subject: weight-sparse models used for qualitative circuit investigations
rows.operation_detail: Qualitatively examined node interpretations, including examples from the pretraining distribution.

conditions.value: pretraining distribution for the reported monosemanticity check

rows.measure: Whether node activations matched a single natural-language interpretation
rows.value: Some but not all nodes were exactly monosemantic on the pretraining distribution.
rows.note: The paper says the Figure 39 node is cherry-picked and that not all nodes are as monosemantic; it gives no proportion.
rows.check: Qualitative claim with no proportion; the example shown is admitted to be cherry-picked.

rows.subject: weight-sparse models
rows.operation_detail: Described the feature composition of circuits, especially for more complex tasks.
rows.measure: Presence of polysemantic nodes or features in the circuits
rows.baseline: Dense models, described as having more of this issue
rows.value: The circuits do not consist entirely of monosemantic nodes or edges; some concepts are spread across several nodes that also perform other tasks, though to a lesser extent than in dense models.
rows.note: This is a qualitative scope statement, not an estimate of the fraction of neurons with one job.
rows.check: A limitations statement, not a measured result.

rows.subject: weight-sparse models
rows.operation_detail: Mean-ablated every node outside the pruned circuit.

conditions.value: mean activation over the pretraining distribution

rows.measure: Task loss after retaining the circuit and ablating other nodes
rows.value: Mean-ablating every node except the circuit preserves task loss.
rows.note: The circuits can include neurons, attention channels, and residual-channel nodes; they are not exclusively neuron-only attribution graphs.
rows.check: Measures circuit sufficiency in small weight-sparse models whose interpretability is induced by training, not in a large model's own neurons, and not via attribution graphs. It does not bear on V5 as stated. The state is observed only for the paper's own claim. Circuits mix neurons, attention channels and residual reads and writes.

rows.subject: weight-sparse models
rows.operation_detail: Ablated nodes that had been identified as part of the circuit while leaving the rest of the network intact.
rows.measure: Task loss after deleting circuit nodes
rows.baseline: Performance with the circuit nodes intact
rows.note: This supports necessity of the identified nodes for the tested task behavior in these sparse models.
rows.check: Necessity of circuit nodes in the same purpose-built sparse models; same mismatch with V5 as r4. The text gives no numeric loss values, only 'severely impaired' and Figure 32.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.

reader_labels.label: limits_scope
reader_labels.condition: Pruned circuits for the paper's hand-crafted tasks in weight-sparse models
reader_labels.reason: Retaining the circuit preserves task loss and ablating its nodes severely impairs performance (r4–r5), but the tested circuits are task-specific, use multiple node types, and are not attribution graphs for a large dense model.
